source: Davis, Logemann, Loveland (1962) A machine program for theorem-proving; Davis and Putnam (1960)
finding: DPLL is the 1962 refinement of the 1960 Davis-Putnam resolution procedure. It replaces resolution by backtracking search with two inference rules: unit propagation and pure-literal elimination. Read via the Wikipedia article only, not the original papers.
numbers: Davis-Putnam: JACM 7(3) 201-215 (1960). DLL: CACM 1962 (the article's intro says 1961, its references say 1962). Worst-case time O(2^n), space O(n) for the basic algorithm.
quote: Efficiency is strongly affected by the choice of the branching literal.
limits: Secondary source. Original papers not read. The article is inconsistent on the DLL year.
agent_relevance: Unit propagation is the cheap forced-move step. The schema can copy it: apply all forced consequences with code before any branching.

source: Wikipedia (2025) DPLL algorithm: algorithm steps
finding: The algorithm loops: propagate units, eliminate pure literals, stop if the formula is empty (SAT) or holds an empty clause (UNSAT), else split on a literal and recurse with short-circuit OR. The article formalises it as five rules: Propagate, Pure, Decide, Backtrack, Fail.
numbers: Five rules. The example figure shows 5 fruitless attempts before success.
limits: Plain DPLL has no learning and no non-chronological backtracking, so it can repeat the same conflict in different branches.
agent_relevance: Maps onto S4 TEST and backtrack: decide, propagate, fail, undo. A failed branch yields nothing reusable unless a lemma is stored.

source: Wikipedia (2025) Conflict-driven clause learning
finding: CDCL extends DPLL with clause learning from each conflict, non-chronological backjumping, restarts that keep learned clauses, and forgetting of redundant clauses. Origin: GRASP (Marques-Silva and Sakallah, ICCAD 1996; IEEE Trans. Computers 48(5), 1999), with Bayardo and Schrag (AAAI 1997) look-back for CSP.
numbers: GRASP 1996 and 1999. Chaff DAC 2001, pp 530-535. Six basic rules plus Forget and Restart; the worked example has 15 steps.
limits: The page does not cover first UIP, VSIDS or watched literals.
agent_relevance: When a check fails, extract a small reusable reason (a lemma) and jump back to the decision that caused it, not just the last one. Matches guardrail G2 (revise from real failing output).

source: Wikipedia (2025) DPLL algorithm: timeline of solver progress
finding: Learning and non-chronological backtracking arrived in 1996 (GRASP). In 2004 and 2005 the SAT competitions were won by zChaff and MiniSat. As of 2019 most state-of-the-art solvers are CDCL-based.
numbers: 1996 GRASP; 2004 zChaff; 2005 MiniSat; 2010-2019 gains from branching policies and propagation data structures.
limits: Secondary source; one item (BDDs for SAT, 1986) is marked citation needed.
agent_relevance: Decades of gains came from learning plus engineering, not from smarter global planning. Supports small cheap steps with rich failure feedback.

source: Moskewicz, Madigan, Zhao, Zhang, Malik (2001) Chaff: Engineering an Efficient SAT Solver
finding: Chaff reaches one to two orders of magnitude speed-up over GRASP and SATO. The authors say it comes from engineering, mainly two-watched-literal Boolean constraint propagation and the VSIDS decision heuristic, not from stronger learning. It also uses restarts.
numbers: Abstract: one to two orders of magnitude on difficult benchmarks. SSS.1.0: about 10x faster, all done within 100 s. SSS.1.0.a: Chaff finished 9 of 9; SATO and GRASP only 2. SSS-SAT.1.0: Chaff finished all 100 in under 1000 s (100 s cap each); SATO aborted 32 of the first 41 tried. VLIW-SAT.1.0: Chaff finished 100 in under 10000 s total; SATO and GRASP aborted 19 of the first 20.
quote: speedup is not the result of sophisticated learning strategies for pruning the search space, but of efficient engineering
limits: Authors' own benchmark runs and configs; they say they could not reproduce one competing GRASP result because configs were unavailable. On easy DIMACS sets (ii, aim, par8) all three solvers tie.
agent_relevance: Speed of the check loop mattered more than clever search. Make every TEST step cheap and mechanical so many more can run.

source: Moskewicz et al. (2001) Chaff: VSIDS definition
finding: VSIDS: each literal has a counter, bumped when it appears in a learned conflict clause. The highest-counter unassigned literal is chosen. All counters are periodically divided by a constant, so recent conflicts weigh most. The rule does not depend on the current assignment, so it is cheap.
numbers: Counters start at 0; periodic division by a constant; ties broken randomly by default.
limits: Heuristic, no optimality proof. Needs restarts to avoid getting stuck in a bad region.
agent_relevance: A recency-weighted tally of what keeps failing is a cheap way to choose where to look next. Fits an impasse detector (G1) that fires on signal.

source: Audemard and Simon (2009) Predicting Learnt Clauses Quality in Modern SAT Solvers
finding: Introduces Literal Block Distance (LBD): the number of distinct decision levels in a learned clause. Low-LBD clauses are used far more often. Keeping them and deleting the rest speeds the solver. Glucose, built on this, solves more instances.
numbers: Mean propagation/conflict uses: LBD 2 clauses 202/1827, LBD 3 50/295, LBD 4 26/136, LBD 5 19/80; length-2 clauses 209/2452. MiniSat variants on the SAT-Race 06 set: original 70 solved (35 SAT, 35 UNSAT), avg time 209; +lbd 79 (47+32), 145; +ag+lbd 82 (45+37), 175. Table 4: Glucose 176 solved (75 SAT, 101 UNSAT); PicoSAT 153; RSAT 139; Minisat+ 136; MiniSat 132; zChaff 2001 84. Glucose 1.7x faster than RSAT on commonly solved instances.
limits: Different benchmark sets and CPU cut-offs (1000 s in the LBD study). Margins vary with the set.
agent_relevance: Which stored lessons to keep can be predicted from a simple structural score. A memory of past failures needs such a pruning rule or it grows without bound.

source: Heule, Kullmann, Marek (2016) Solving and Verifying the boolean Pythagorean Triples problem via Cube-and-Conquer
finding: SAT proves that {1..7825} cannot be 2-coloured without a monochromatic Pythagorean triple; a valid colouring exists for {1..7664}. Cube-and-Conquer (look-ahead split then CDCL) solved it, and a checkable DRAT proof was produced.
numbers: About 4 CPU years (21,900 CPU hours splitting, 13,200 CPU hours solving); 800 cores, about 2 days. Proof about 200 TB; compressed certificate 68 GB. Blocked-clause elimination cut F7825 from 6494 vars and 18944 clauses to 3745 vars and 14672 clauses. First split into about 10^6 cubes.
quote: solve the problem on a cluster with 800 cores in about 2 days
limits: One instance, huge compute. The proof size means few can recheck it. Symmetry breaking was needed.
agent_relevance: A proof object an independent checker accepts. A negative answer, not just a found witness, can be made checkable (G3 and the verifier idea).

source: Heule et al. (2016) Pythagorean triples: proof pipeline and verification
finding: The solver emits a DRAT refutation for each cube. These are joined with proofs for the tautology transformation, symmetry breaking and cube splitting, and an independent checker validates the whole chain. An incremental solver reuses learned clauses across sub-cubes.
numbers: Two-level splitting; billions of sub-cubes per cube; symmetry broken on variable x2520 (the most occurring).
limits: Verification cost is itself large.
agent_relevance: Design pattern: separate untrusted fast search from a small trusted checker. Guardrail G3 asks for the same split.

source: Selsam, Lamm, Bunz, Liang, Dill (2019) Learning a SAT Solver from Single-Bit Supervision (NeuroSAT)
finding: A message-passing neural net trained only on a satisfiable/unsatisfiable bit learns to find satisfying assignments. Trained on SR(U(10,40)) and tested on SR(40) with 26 iterations, it gets 85% overall accuracy and decodes a solution for 70% of satisfiable problems.
numbers: Overall 85%; accuracy on unsat 96%; on sat 73%; solved 70% (Table 1, columns re-read after garbled extraction). SR(40): 40 variables, almost 200 clauses, pairs differ by one literal in a thousand. Trained on millions of problems. With more rounds, 25% of satisfiable SR(200) problems solved; under 10% if limited to the training iteration count. On 4,888 satisfiable problems (of 7,200 generated) from graph tasks, decoded solutions for 85%; Survey Propagation converged on none.
limits: Does not beat modern solvers; small random SAT. An LSTM baseline could not exceed 50% on its training set.
agent_relevance: Learned scorers can detect satisfiability from structure but are weak against exact solvers. Argues for using a real solver as the check, not a model judgement (G1, G2).

source: Selsam et al. (2019) NeuroSAT: NeuroUNSAT and unsat cores
finding: Trained on a distribution where each unsatisfiable problem has a small unsat core, the network (NeuroUNSAT) predicts satisfiability with 100% accuracy by recognising the core.
numbers: 100% test accuracy on SRC(30, PP(3,2)); the core literals fall in their own cluster 98% of the time.
limits: The authors do not expect it to generalise to arbitrary unsat cores. Pattern recognition, not proof.
agent_relevance: A model can learn to point at the minimal failing part. Scaffold equivalent: ask for a minimal failing subset, then have code check it.

source: Selsam et al. (2019) NeuroSAT: context against classical solvers
finding: MiniSAT needs about ten backjumps and over a hundred unit propagations per SR(40) problem, which shows the task is not trivial. The authors are only cautiously optimistic that learned guidance could help solvers.
numbers: Ten backjumps on average; more than 100 unit propagations; Survey Propagation (Knuth 2015 variant, own implementation) 0 of the structured problems versus NeuroSAT 85%.
limits: Authors' own SP baseline.
agent_relevance: Learned heuristics may guide where to look, but a classical solver still decides.

source: Hazra, Venturato, Zuidberg Dos Martires, De Raedt (2024) Can Large Language Models Reason? A Characterization via 3-SAT
finding: GPT-4 follows the easy-hard-easy shape of random 3-SAT: good far from the threshold, poor in the hard region. The authors read this as shortcuts, not true reasoning. An external solver fixes it.
numbers: GPT-4 accuracy on SAT Search falls to about 10% in the hard region. Changing the input from CNF to a menu story did not help. SAT-Translate (LLM writes the CNF, MiniSAT solves) gives about 100% over the whole alpha range.
quote: LLMs are incapable of performing true reasoning, as required for solving 3-SAT problems.
limits: GPT-4 era models; instances small (n at most 10); even in easy regions GPT-4 is not perfect.
agent_relevance: Strongest practical lesson: let the model translate, let a solver solve. The model is good at formalising, poor at search. Supports the rule that code, not the model, decides.

source: Hazra et al. (2025) Have Large Language Models Learned to Reason? A Characterization via 3-SAT Phase Transition
finding: All tested LLMs show the inverted phase transition on SAT Search, with a drop to about 10% in the hard region, except DeepSeek-R1, which beats the others and whose traces show backtracking, unit propagation, heuristic choice and self-correction.
numbers: About 5000 random formulas, n up to 10, alpha 1.1 to 11.0; mean n 7.2, mean m 33, mean alpha 4.7. Labelled by MiniSAT 2.2; model counts by D4. Non-R1 hard-region accuracy about 10%. R1 hard-region accuracy exceeds other LLMs easy-region accuracy. In-context examples did not help the hard region. Accuracy rises with satisfiability ratio (model count / 2^n).
limits: Tiny formulas. R1 often stops early without exploring the whole tree: sound on SAT but incomplete. R1 is tied to familiar input formats. Other LLMs mostly fail to classify unsat instances.
agent_relevance: Reasoning-trained models search with backtracking in text, but incompletely. Treat a text search as a hint and confirm with a solver or counted check.

source: Hazra et al. (2025) R1 search behaviour and token growth
finding: R1 output tokens grow polynomially with input size, and thinking tokens rise in the hard region. GPT-4o does greedy search with no backtracking and its output length stays roughly flat. R1 failure modes: stopping before the tree is exhausted, unit-propagation mistakes after backtracking, treating unset variables as set.
numbers: Output vs input tokens: polynomial for R1, roughly constant for others (Appendix Fig 14). Worked trace shows a unit-propagation mistake at step 14.
limits: Qualitative trace reading by the authors; no inter-rater numbers.
agent_relevance: More thinking budget on hard items is sound only if a signal says hard (G1). Hardness is measurable here: clause-to-variable ratio near 4.27.

source: Pan, Ganesh, Abernethy, Esposo, Lee (2025) Can Transformers Reason Logically? A Study in SAT Solving
finding: Proof by construction that a decoder-only Transformer with O(p^2) parameters and chain-of-thought can decide all 3-SAT instances with at most p variables and c clauses, simulating DPLL-style assumption, deduction and backtracking. A compiled model is perfect; a trained one learns it at seen sizes but not larger ones.
numbers: Compiled PyTorch model: 100% on all evaluation sets. Trained models (6-10 and 11-15 variables), SAT vs UNSAT accuracy 99.8% or higher in the same-size setting; full trace correct 99.1% to 100%. Length generalisation fails: accuracy drops as variable counts go up to 20, with lowest cells 88.7% and 86.1% in one table.
limits: Non-uniform model of computation. Training on algorithmic traces, not natural text.
agent_relevance: CoT can carry DPLL in principle, but learned versions do not scale in size. Another reason to keep the search loop in code.

source: Wei, Wu, Wan et al. (2025) SATBench: Benchmarking LLMs' Logical Reasoning via Automated Puzzle Generation from SAT Formulas
finding: 2,100 story puzzles built from SAT formulas with a controlled number of clauses. Accuracy falls as clauses grow. UNSAT is far harder than SAT for all models.
numbers: Zero-shot overall: o4-mini 89.3, DeepSeek-R1 87.8, DeepSeek-V3 84.0, Claude 3.7 Sonnet 74.8, gpt-4o 58.0, gpt-4o-mini 53.9. Average over models: easy 78.5, medium 59.8, hard 53.0 (random 50). Hard UNSAT: o4-mini 65.0, R1 83.6, V3 74.3, Claude 3.7 42.1, gpt-4o 18.9. Average hard SAT 66.7 vs hard UNSAT 39.3. Easy 4-19 clauses, medium 20-30, hard 31-50. Human validation pass rate above 90%.
limits: Story puzzles mix parsing and search errors. GPT-4o judges the traces. Scores below 50% on hard UNSAT come from claiming SAT.
agent_relevance: Models lean to saying satisfiable. A no-solution claim needs an exhaustive check, so do not accept it from the model alone.

source: Wei et al. (2025) SATBench error analysis
finding: Main errors: satisfiability bias, context inconsistency (contradicting earlier steps), condition omission (ignoring clauses) and spurious priors. SAT is an existential claim and UNSAT a universal one, which the authors give as the reason for the gap.
numbers: Error shares, o4-mini vs DeepSeek-R1: satisfiability bias 68.7% vs 40.5%; context inconsistency 17.0% vs 44.7%; condition omission 14.3% vs 12.6%. Trace validity: o4-mini 74.4, R1 78.0.
limits: Error classes assigned by GPT-4o, then spot-checked.
agent_relevance: Condition omission and drift are what a counted checklist catches. Let code re-check each clause against the proposed assignment.

source: Zhang, Chen, Chen (2026) Satisfiability Solving with LLMs: A Matched-Pair Evaluation of Reasoning Capability
finding: Plain accuracy on SAT is misleading: many models score high by calling most formulas satisfiable, miss the easy-hard-easy shape, and degrade sharply with more variables. The measure ADR (both members of a minimally different SAT/UNSAT pair correct) separates reasoning models from guessers.
numbers: More than 2,700 3-SAT formulas; 70 SAT/UNSAT pairs per setting. GPT-5 ADR 0.79 at 25 variables and 0.35 at 50 (only about 20% of runs finished at 50). One test: precision 0.78, recall 0.76, F1 0.77, accuracy 0.77, yet ADR 0.60. Across CNF, Vertex Cover and 3D packing, decisions agree on more than 80% of instances for most models.
limits: Results depend on the pair generator. GPT-5 timeouts at larger n shrink the sample. FSE 2026; preprint read.
agent_relevance: Use paired checks: believe a claim only if the model also gets the near-twin counter case right. A ready design for S4 TEST (G3, mutated input).

source: Zhang, Chen, Chen (2026) paired formulas: which models track the phase transition
finding: GPT-5 is the only model whose curve qualitatively follows the classical easy-hard-easy shape. Reasoning-oriented models (GPT-5, o1, o3-mini, deepseek-reasoner) do better. For alpha above 5, precision for almost all models collapses to near 0, with GPT-5 and deepseek-reasoner the outliers.
numbers: Most models show a strong bias to predict SAT. Variable counts up to 75 for some runs.
limits: API runs in a fixed window; curves read from figures.
agent_relevance: Use reasoning models for logical judgement, and still back them with a solver.

source: Monasson, Zecchina, Kirkpatrick, Selman, Troyansky (1999) 2+p-SAT: Relation of Typical-Case Complexity to the Nature of the Phase Transition
finding: Random K-SAT has a SAT/UNSAT phase transition. For K=2 it is continuous (threshold alpha=1); for K=3 it is discontinuous (random first-order). The backbone of frozen variables appears abruptly for K=3, which explains why DPLL-style search blows up: early wrong choices on backbone variables cost long backtracking.
numbers: 2+p-SAT mixes 2- and 3-clauses: continuous transition for p below p0 = 0.41, discontinuous above. Finite-size runs with N from 50 to 500.
quote: early mistakes by mis-asserting a backbone spin, and take a long time to backtrack to correct their mistakes
limits: Physics-style replica method, not rigorous for K=3. Large-N claims rest on extrapolation.
agent_relevance: Hard instances sit near the threshold where many variables are frozen. The clause ratio is a measurable hardness signal for when to spend extra budget.

source: Ding, Sly, Sun (2022) Proof of the satisfiability conjecture for large k
finding: For all k at least an absolute constant k0, a random k-SAT formula is satisfiable w.h.p. below a threshold density and unsatisfiable above it. The threshold equals the one-step replica symmetry breaking prediction from physics. Method: moment calculations mapped to tree recursions.
numbers: Rigorous only for large k. Arxiv v3 dated 2021 (journal year 2022 from memory).
limits: Does not settle k=3 (numerically about 4.267, as cited in Hazra 2025).
agent_relevance: Confirms the clause-ratio threshold as a real structural feature; anchors the alpha sweeps in the LLM studies.

source: Mitchell, Selman, Levesque (1992) Hard and easy distributions of SAT problems
finding: Random 3-SAT: the hardest instances for DPLL sit near a clause-to-variable ratio of about 4.3, where about half are satisfiable; far below or above they are easy. Not opened; the claim is echoed by the Hazra and Monasson papers I read.
numbers: Peak near alpha about 4.26 to 4.3, shown again by Kirkpatrick and Selman (Science 1994).
limits: Not opened. Number from memory and indirect support only.
agent_relevance: Original source of the hardness-versus-ratio picture that the LLM studies now reuse.

source: Cook (1971) The complexity of theorem-proving procedures
finding: SAT is the first NP-complete problem: every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time. Not opened; Heule et al. (2016) say the same in their introduction, which I read.
numbers: STOC 1971; Levin proved a similar result independently.
limits: Not opened; no numbers.
agent_relevance: Any finite-domain check can be encoded as SAT, so a SAT solver is a general verifier for small structured claims.

source: Marques-Silva and Sakallah (1996, 1999) GRASP: a search algorithm for propositional satisfiability
finding: Put conflict analysis, learned clauses and non-chronological backtracking into DPLL, creating CDCL. Not opened; dates and content come from the Wikipedia pages I read.
numbers: ICCAD 1996 pp 220-227; IEEE Trans. Computers 48(5) 506-521, 1999.
limits: Not opened. Chaff reports 1-2 orders of magnitude over GRASP, which is the measured follow-on.
agent_relevance: The failing run itself yields a lesson, which is what G2 asks for.

source: Een and Sorensson (2003) An extensible SAT-solver (MiniSat)
finding: MiniSat is a small CDCL solver, the base of Glucose and the labeller in Hazra et al. (2024, 2025). Not opened (PDF text unreadable).
numbers: MiniSat v2.2 labels all instances in Hazra 2025; won in 2005 per Wikipedia.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: A tiny trusted solver is enough to label ground truth when evaluating the agent.

source: Cross-study limits of LLM SAT evidence (Hazra 2025, Wei 2025, Zhang 2026)
finding: Formulas are small (n at most 10 in Hazra; up to about 75 in Zhang) and random, not the structured industrial instances where CDCL excels. The 2026 critique shows plain accuracy overstates ability because of the SAT-guessing bias.
numbers: SATBench hard UNSAT average 39.3% (below chance) while overall hard average is 53.0%; Zhang ADR 0.60 against accuracy 0.77 in one test.
limits: Different benchmarks, prompts and judges; not directly comparable.
agent_relevance: Report class-wise or paired results and include the guess-SAT baseline when evaluating our scaffold on logic tasks.
